recipe.history:
The beet, Beta vulgaris, is native to the coastlines of the Mediterranean and Atlantic Europe, where wild sea beet grew in the intertidal zones and was harvested by humans since prehistoric times. Ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans consumed beet leaves as a vegetable and prized the roots for medicinal use. The Romans were the first to cultivate beet roots of meaningful size for food, and Roman cookbooks describe preparations using roots cooked with mustard, vinegar, and oil in ways that would be recognizable today. Through the Middle Ages, beet roots remained a staple of European peasant cooking — hearty, sweet, readily stored through winter, and capable of being preserved in vinegar or fermented. The beet's most dramatic transformation came in the 18th century when German and French chemists discovered that the sugar beet variety could be processed into crystalline sugar — a discovery that reshaped European agriculture and gave rise to the modern sugar beet industry. Meanwhile, the garden beet continued its quieter cultivation in Eastern European cuisines — Russian borscht, Polish ćwikła, Ukrainian vinegret — where it became so deeply embedded that the red-purple color of beet juice functions almost as a cultural symbol across the region. The Chioggia beet, with its candy-striped pink and white interior, and the golden beet, milder and less assertive than its red cousin, represent the biodiversity that survives from centuries of varietal selection across European farming traditions.

Beets entered the American burger conversation along two tracks: the health-food movement and the antipodean influence. In Australia and New Zealand, the canned beet slice on a burger has been standard practice since at least the mid-20th century — the Aussie burger with egg, bacon, pineapple, and beet is a national institution — and this tradition had an outsized influence on American craft burger culture when Australian food media and chefs gained international visibility in the 2000s. Simultaneously, the American health-food and juice bar culture of the 1990s and 2000s brought roasted beet into mainstream American restaurant usage, where its earthy sweetness, brilliant color, and substantial texture made it a compelling topping for ambitious burgers. Roasted beet on a burger functions as the dominant, dramatic element: its deep red-purple bleeds into every surface it touches, its sweet earthiness contrasts with the savory fat of the beef, and its tender, almost silky texture provides a textural complement to the chew of a well-built patty. A beet burger is a statement. It is not a shy dish.

Beets and I got off to a rocky start because the first beets I ate were from a can, and canned beets are to fresh roasted beets what instant coffee is to a pour-over. I ate them reluctantly at a school cafeteria and formed a prejudice that lasted until my mid-twenties, when I ate roasted golden beets at a farm dinner in upstate New York. They had been roasted whole in foil with a little olive oil and thyme, then peeled and served warm with crumbled chèvre and a drizzle of balsamic. I ate four servings and spent the drive home recalibrating my entire understanding of the ingredient. The red beets followed soon after, and the beet burger followed them. I have since apologized to the beet, privately, on multiple occasions.

A beet burger requires the cook's full discipline, because the visual drama of roasted beet on a burger can create the illusion that the appearance is the achievement. It is not. The achievement is the medium rare patty — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, pink at the center, fat rendered and fluid, juices intact — that sits beneath the beet and provides the savory, beefy backbone without which the beet's sweetness has nothing to play against. A well-done patty under a pile of roasted beets produces a sweet, dry mouthful that resolves into nothing. A medium rare patty under the same beets produces a conversation: the beet's earthy sweetness, the beef's rich savoriness, the rendered fat rounding everything together into a bite that is more than the sum of its parts. The two left feet of this burger are the beet and the beef. They only dance well together when the temperature is right.
ingredients: Kosher salt and cracked black pepper
3 medium red beets, trimmed and scrubbed (greens reserved if desired)
1 medium golden beet, trimmed and scrubbed
4 oz sharp white cheddar or aged goat gouda, sliced
instructions: 1. Make the rye-wheat buns: Activate yeast in warm water and milk with 1 tsp sugar, 5–7 minutes until foamy. Combine bread flour, rye flour, remaining sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with dough hook.

2. Add yeast mixture, molasses, and egg. Mix on low until a shaggy dough forms. Add softened butter in pieces. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes — the dough will be slightly stickier than a pure wheat dough due to the rye; this is correct.
3. Cover and let rise 1.5–2 hours until doubled. Rye slows fermentation; be patient.
4. Divide into 6 portions, shape into rounds, and proof on parchment-lined baking sheets 45–60 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with caraway seeds if using. Bake 16–18 minutes until dark golden. Cool on a rack.

6. Roast the beets: Preheat oven to 400°F. Toss trimmed beets with olive oil, thyme, salt, and pepper. Wrap each variety separately in foil (to prevent the red beets from staining the golden beet) and place on a baking sheet. Roast 50–60 minutes until completely tender when pierced with a knife. Cool until handleable, then peel by rubbing with paper towels — the skins will slip off. Slice into rounds approximately 1/4 inch thick. Toss with balsamic vinegar and season lightly.

7. Make the horseradish crème fraîche: Stir together crème fraîche, horseradish, lemon juice, salt, white pepper, and chives. Taste — it should be tangy, creamy, and have a clean heat from the horseradish. Refrigerate until needed.
8. Cook the bacon: In a skillet over medium heat, cook bacon strips until crispy. Drain on paper towels. Reserve.

9. Form patties: Gently combine ground chuck and short rib. Divide into 4 portions (~6 oz each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a thumb indent in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and lay cheddar or aged goat gouda slices on each. Cook 2–2.5 minutes more. Pull at 130–132°F and rest loosely foil-tented 3–4 minutes to reach 133–135°F.
11. Toast bun halves in butter until golden.

12. Assemble: Spread horseradish crème fraîche generously on both cut bun faces. Place microgreens or watercress on the bottom bun. Set the rested, cheese-topped patty on the greens. Lay 1–2 strips of crispy bacon over the patty. Arrange 2–3 rounds of roasted beet (a mix of red and golden) on top of the bacon. Close with the top bun and serve immediately, with extra balsamic-dressed beet rounds on the side if desired.
